title: The fish who prayed for rain
hookLine: a fish king makes the rain fall by an act of truth (Jataka 75)

cards: Cracked mud, in plates, where the water used to be. Each day the edge pulls back a little further. The fish crowd into what's left, and the crows and herons stand at the edge, waiting.
In this Jataka tale, the Buddha in an earlier life is one of those fish, the king of the pond. He can't fly away or dig a well. He has one thing left to offer, and it isn't a plea or a bargain.
It's a sentence that happens to be true.

teach.b: First, the drought. The tale sets it in the kingdom of Kosala. No rain comes, the crops wither, and the pond goes to mud.
The birds are picking the fish off one by one. Second, the fish king rises.
He pushes up out of the mud, looks at the sky, and calls on Pajjunna, the god of the rain clouds in the story.

But he doesn't ask for a favor. Third, the act of truth. In Pali it's called sacca-kiriya: a person states something true about their own life, sets it out like an offering, and the truth itself carries power.
The fish king's truth: though he was born among fish, who eat one another, he has never, as far back as he can remember, taken the life of any creature.
If that is true, he says, let the rain fall. And it does. The clouds gather, the pond fills, and the fish are saved.
The act of truth only works because it's true. The fish can't bluff the sky; whatever power his words have comes from the life standing behind them.
He doesn't promise to be good from now on, or describe the fish he hopes to be. He points to what he has already done, plainly, and lets it speak.
Some readers hear a quiet question in the tale: what could you say about your own life that's simply true? Not impressive. Just true enough to stand on.

how: The act of truth appears elsewhere in the Pali texts too: in the Angulimala Sutta, Angulimala speaks a true sentence about his own life as a blessing for a woman in labor, and those words are chanted as a protective verse.

o: an act of truth, a true word set out
a prayer begging the gods for rain
a promise to be good from now on

games.q: the fish king's tale: tap the pairs.

s: the fish king begs the rain-god for a favor
he doesn't bargain. he states a truth about his life and asks the rain to fall if it's true.
his truth is that he has never taken a life
though born among fish that eat each other, he says he has never killed a creature.
an act of truth works even if the words are false
the power of the words comes from the life behind them.

games.q: you're the fish king. the pond is nearly mud and the herons are waiting. what do you do?
o: burrow deep and wait it out.
rise up and speak one true thing to the sky.
lead the fish toward the far bank.
games.why: he calls on the rain-god with an act of truth: he has never taken a life. the rain falls and fills the pond.

practice: Feel the breath come and go a few times, then look for something about your life that's plainly true: I kept a promise this week; I'm tired today; I love my brother.
Say it out loud, quietly, once, and sit with how it sounds in the room. Is it solid, or does it need anything added?

wordCard.voice: Sacca-kiriya. An act of truth: a fish king in a dying pond speaks one plain truth about his life, and the rain falls. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: sacca-kiriya, an act of truth; sacca is truth, kiriya an act.

carryVoice: Your line: an act of truth. Plain, sure, and yours. That's day eight hundred twenty-seven.
